title: The white elephant dream
hook: Queen Maya dreams a white elephant enters her side; the wise men say a great son is coming

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Dhammapada, and camp one closed with twenty-one words. Your line was what you think, you become. Did you catch a thought you keep repeating? Day twenty-two.
screen: `THE DHAMMAPADA — WHAT YOU THINK, YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: Camp two. The stories. From today, the Buddha's whole life, told like a serial, one scene a day, from the palace to the forest to the last night under the trees. And it starts, like a lot of great stories, with a dream. A city called Kapilavatthu, at the foot of the Himalayas. It's the time of a summer festival. Queen Maya, wife of King Suddhodana, has kept the festival well, given gifts, and gone to sleep. And in the night she dreams that a white elephant, shining like silver, walks toward her, circles her bed, and enters her side.
screen: `CAMP TWO: THE STORIES.` → `A CITY BELOW THE MOUNTAINS.` → `A QUEEN DREAMS OF AN ELEPHANT.`

segments.voice: Here's how the later tellings go on. In the dream, Maya is carried by guardian spirits up to a high place in the mountains, bathed in a lake, and laid on a heavenly couch. Then a white elephant with six tusks, holding a white lotus in its trunk, comes down from a golden mountain, trumpets, walks around her three times, and seems to enter her right side. In the morning she tells the king. He calls in the wise men, the brahmins who read signs, and asks what it means. Their answer: be glad. The queen has conceived, and it's a son. If he stays in the household, he'll become a great king who rules the world. If he leaves it, he'll become a buddha, one who wakes up and removes the veil from the world. It's worth being clear about where this comes from. The oldest discourses describe the Buddha's conception with wonders, a great light, the earth trembling, but they don't mention the elephant. The dream comes from later biographies and commentaries, and it has been loved for more than two thousand years: it's carved on some of the oldest Buddhist monuments in India. Why an elephant? In ancient India a white elephant was a royal treasure, rare and auspicious, a sign of strength, gentleness and greatness at once. Across Buddhist Asia the dream is painted on temple walls, and in Thailand and Myanmar the white elephant is still a sign of blessing. The story is doing what beginnings do. Before anyone knows who this child will be, something announces him.
screen: `A LAKE IN THE MOUNTAINS.` · `SIX TUSKS AND A WHITE LOTUS.` · `A KING, OR A BUDDHA.` · `A LATER TELLING, CARVED IN STONE.` · then, large: `SOME THINGS ANNOUNCE THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: From today, the bell gives you two minutes. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Then recall a dream that stayed with you. Not one you've analyzed, just one that stayed. Maybe from childhood, maybe from last month. Let its pictures come back: the colors, the place, the feeling when you woke. You don't need to decide what it meant. Just notice that some things arrive in us before we understand them. When your mind wanders, come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The white elephant dream. Queen Maya's dream before the Buddha's birth: a white elephant, six tusks, a lotus, and a son who would be a king or a buddha.
Your line: some things announce themselves. Today, notice one small sign of something beginning: a bud, a new habit, a first conversation. Day twenty-two.

screen: `DAY 22 COUNTS. CAMP TWO BEGINS.` → `TOMORROW: BORN IN A GROVE.`

howItsDone: Buddhists remember Maya's dream in temple murals, carvings and festival plays; in many countries the story is told to children as the first chapter of the Buddha's life, and the white elephant remains a symbol of blessing.

fork.setup: you're King Suddhodana. your queen has dreamed a white elephant entered her side. what do you do?
options: ignore it. it's only a dream.
call the wise men to read it.
send the queen away to rest.
fork.reveal: he calls the brahmins. they tell him to be glad: a son is coming, who will be a great king, or, if he leaves home, a buddha.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy-tale opening.
what it means: the first scene of the Buddha's life story, a sign that something great is coming before anyone understands it.

what a scholar hears: the dream is told in the Nidanakatha, the introduction to the Jataka commentary, and in Sanskrit biographies; the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (MN 123) describes the conception's wonders without it. early reliefs at Bharhut show the scene.

notes: Details of the dream (four guardian kings, Anotatta lake, silver mountain / golden mansion, six tusks, white lotus, circling three times, right side) follow the Nidanakatha as remembered; the script simplifies. Rhys Davids translated the Nidanakatha in Buddhist Birth Stories (1880), but nothing is quoted. Confirm.
The brahmins' interpretation (king or buddha) is from the Nidanakatha; the same prophecy appears again at the naming (day 26). Confirm no clash.
Bharhut relief of Maya's dream: confirm (the trapdoor names Bharhut).
